summary: Sirach opens by saying that all wisdom comes from the Lord, existed before all things, and remains beyond full human searching. The chapter then links wisdom repeatedly with “the fear of the Lord,” describing its gladness, fullness, crown, and root. It closes with practical warnings about wrath, patience, commandments, hypocrisy, self-exaltation, and deceit.
whyItMatters: This chapter sets the book’s starting point: wisdom is God’s gift, not merely cleverness or information. It also introduces the repeated pattern by which reverence for God is tested in speech, patience, humility, and obedience.

context.author: Yeshua (Jesus) son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; his unnamed grandson later translated the Hebrew book into Greek in Egypt.
context.audience: Originally students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem; through the Greek translation, Greek-reading Jews in Egypt or the wider diaspora.
context.date: The Hebrew work was composed in the early second century BC, likely around 180–175 BC; the Greek translation followed after the grandson came to Egypt, commonly understood as 132 BC.
context.setting: Jerusalem under Hellenistic rule, with temple worship, scribal learning, and Greek-speaking Mediterranean pressures in the background.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction in poetic maxims and paired lines; chapter 1 functions as an opening meditation on wisdom, reverence, and disciplined conduct.

outline.heading: Wisdom’s Source And Mystery
outline.note: Wisdom comes from the Lord and reaches beyond what humans can count or search out; verses 5 and 7 are blank in the World English Bible.

outline.heading: The Lord Gives Wisdom
outline.note: The Lord alone is wise, creates wisdom, measures her, and gives her freely to those who love him.

outline.heading: The Fear Of The Lord
outline.note: The chapter repeats that fear of the Lord is glory, joy, beginning, fullness, crown, and root of wisdom.

outline.heading: Wrath, Patience, And Speech
outline.note: Verse 21 is blank in the World English Bible. The following sayings contrast unjust wrath with patience, timely speech, and the treasures of wisdom.

outline.heading: Commandments And Integrity
outline.note: The final sayings connect the desire for wisdom with keeping commandments and warn against a double heart, hypocrisy, self-exaltation, and deceit.

keyVerses.text: All wisdom comes from the Lord, and is with him forever.
keyVerses.why: This opening sentence states the chapter’s basic claim about wisdom’s source and permanence.

keyVerses.text: There is one wise, greatly to be feared, sitting upon his throne: the Lord.
keyVerses.why: The verse concentrates the chapter’s language about wisdom, fear, rule, and the Lord in one statement.

keyVerses.text: To fear the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. It was created together with the faithful in the womb.
keyVerses.why: This is one of the chapter’s repeated definitions linking wisdom with the fear of the Lord.

keyVerses.text: If you desire wisdom, keep the commandments and the Lord will give her to you freely;
keyVerses.why: The verse turns the chapter from description of wisdom to the reader’s concrete response.

themes: Fear of the Lord as wisdom’s beginning

questions.question: What does the chapter mean when it says all wisdom comes from the Lord?
questions.answer: The chapter begins by locating wisdom’s source in the Lord rather than in human discovery alone. It also says wisdom is “with him forever,” which places wisdom before and beyond ordinary human achievement. The chapter later says the Lord gives wisdom freely to those who love him and to those who keep the commandments.

questions.question: Why does the chapter ask questions about sand, rain, sky, earth, and the deep?
questions.answer: These questions emphasize human limits. If no one can count the sand, drops of rain, or days of eternity, then wisdom also exceeds ordinary human measurement. The point is not to give a scientific inventory, but to place wisdom among realities too vast to master.

questions.question: Who is “her” in this chapter?
questions.answer: “Her” refers to wisdom. The chapter speaks of wisdom as something created, measured, poured out, trusted, and held fast. This personified language is part of the book’s wisdom style, but the chapter still says wisdom comes from the Lord and is given by him.

questions.question: What is “the fear of the Lord” here?
questions.answer: Within this chapter, the phrase is connected with glory, gladness, wisdom, instruction, faith, humility, and keeping the commandments. It should not be reduced to panic or terror, because the same passage says it delights the heart and gives joy. The chapter presents it as a reverent orientation toward God that shapes conduct.

questions.question: Are the blessings about long life and things going well meant as a simple guarantee?
questions.answer: The chapter does say that fear of the Lord is linked with “length of days,” blessing, peace, and flourishing. Readers differ on how to read such wisdom sayings: some hear them as general moral instruction about the shape of a wise life, while others may read them more directly as promises. The chapter itself states the connection but does not answer every case where the righteous suffer or die young.

questions.question: Why are verses 5, 7 and 21 blank in this edition?
questions.answer: The World English Bible leaves verses 5, 7 and 21 blank. Sirach survives in different textual forms, and editions can differ in wording and verse numbering. Other editions may include additional lines or number the passage differently.

questions.question: What does the chapter say about anger?
questions.answer: It gives a sharp warning: “Unjust wrath can never be justified.” The reason given is that wrath tips the scale toward the angry person’s downfall. The next verses contrast that with patience, restraint, and speech kept for the right moment.

questions.question: Why does wisdom involve speech and the lips?
questions.answer: The chapter links wisdom with timing and self-control. A patient person hides words until the right moment, and many later tell of his understanding. The final warnings also tell the reader not to be a hypocrite and to keep watch over the lips, so wisdom is shown in what a person says and withholds.

questions.question: What is the danger of coming with a “double heart”?
questions.answer: The phrase appears in a warning not to disobey the fear of the Lord or approach him with divided intention. The chapter pairs it with hypocrisy, self-exaltation, hidden secrets, and a heart full of deceit. Its concern is not merely private feeling, but a mismatch between outward religious posture and inward loyalty.

glossary.def: In this chapter, wisdom is a gift from the Lord, beyond full human searching, and connected with understanding, prudence, instruction, and faithful conduct.
A repeated phrase in the chapter for reverent allegiance to the Lord, shown through wisdom, joy, humility, commandments, patience, and integrity.
Careful understanding or practical judgment; verse 4 pairs it with wisdom from everlasting.
A divided or deceitful inner posture; the chapter warns against coming to the Lord this way.
